We present an x-ray spectromicroscopic investigation of single-crystalline magnetic FeMn/Co bilayers on Cu(001), using X-ray magnetic circular (XMCD) and linear (XMLD) dichroism at the Co and Fe L3 absorption edges in combination with photoelectron emission microscopy (PEEM). Using the magnetic coupling between the ferromagnetic Co layer and the antiferromagnetic FeMn layer we are able to produce magnetic domains with two different crystallographic orientations of the magnetic easy axis within the same sample at the same time. We find a huge difference in the XMLD contrast between the two types of magnetic domains, which we discuss in terms of intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy of XMLD of the Co layer. We also demonstrate that due to the high sensitivity of the method, the small number of induced ferromagnetic Fe moments at the FeMn-Co interface is sufficient to obtain magnetic contrast from XMLD in a metallic system.

# X-ray Spectromicroscopic Investigation of Magnetic Coupling in FeMn/Co Bilayers on Cu(001)

## Introduction and Experimental Approach

This study presents a comprehensive x-ray spectromicroscopic investigation of single-crystalline magnetic bilayers composed of FeMn and Co grown on a Cu(001) substrate. The experimental methodology combines two complementary x-ray magnetic contrast mechanisms—x-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) and x-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD)—measured at the Co and Fe L3 absorption edges. These spectroscopic techniques are integrated with photoemission electron microscopy (PEEM), enabling direct real-space imaging of magnetic domain structures with elemental specificity and high spatial resolution.

## Engineering Dual Crystallographic Domain Orientations

A central achievement of this work lies in exploiting the intrinsic magnetic exchange coupling that exists between the ferromagnetic (FM) Co layer and the antiferromagnetic (AFM) FeMn layer. By carefully controlling this interlayer coupling, the researchers were able to simultaneously stabilize magnetic domains possessing two distinct crystallographic orientations of the easy magnetic axis within a single sample structure. This capability is particularly valuable, as it allows for direct, side-by-side comparison of the magnetic and spectroscopic properties associated with different easy-axis orientations under identical growth and measurement conditions, eliminating sample-to-sample variability as a confounding factor.

## Anisotropic XMLD Contrast in the Co Layer

A key experimental finding is the observation of a pronounced difference in XMLD contrast between the two types of domains corresponding to the different crystallographic easy-axis orientations. This contrast variation is attributed to the intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy inherent in the XMLD response of the Co layer itself. This result underscores the sensitivity of XMLD not only to the magnetic state of the material but also to the underlying crystallographic symmetry and orientation-dependent electronic structure, providing a rich source of information for probing anisotropic magnetic interactions in thin-film systems.

## Detection of Induced Interfacial Moments in Fe

Perhaps the most technically demanding aspect of this investigation is the detection of magnetic contrast arising from the induced ferromagnetic moments present at the FeMn-Co interface. These induced moments in the Fe atoms, which arise as a consequence of the proximity coupling to the adjacent ferromagnetic Co layer, involve only a small fraction of the total Fe atoms at the interface region. Despite the inherently weak signal associated with such a minority species, the high sensitivity of the combined XMLD-PEEM technique successfully resolved this subtle magnetic contrast, demonstrating the method's capability to probe interfacial magnetic phenomena that would otherwise be challenging to access through conventional characterization techniques.

## Significance and Broader Implications

Collectively, these results establish that XMLD can serve as an effective and reliable probe for magnetic contrast in metallic systems, even in the challenging scenario where the ferromagnetic signal originates predominantly from small, induced interfacial moments rather than from a bulk ferromagnetic phase. This finding has significant implications for the broader field of spintronics and magnetic thin-film research, as it validates XMLD-PEEM as a powerful tool for investigating interfacial magnetism, exchange coupling phenomena, and induced moment effects in complex multilayer systems—phenomena that are of central importance to the design and optimization of exchange-bias-based spintronic devices.

# Magnetic Domain Imaging in FeMn/Co Bilayers: Exploiting XMCD and XMLD for Crystallographic and Interfacial Sensitivity

## Introduction

The exchange coupling between ferromagnetic (FM) and antiferromagnetic (AFM) materials continues to attract significant attention due to its fundamental importance in spintronic applications, particularly in the design of spin valves and magnetic tunnel junctions where exchange bias phenomena are exploited to pin magnetic layers. Understanding the microscopic mechanisms governing this coupling requires characterization techniques capable of resolving both the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic domain structures with high spatial and chemical resolution. In this study, we present a comprehensive investigation of single-crystalline FeMn/Co bilayers grown epitaxially on Cu(001) substrates, employing complementary X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) and X-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD) techniques in combination with photoelectron emission microscopy (PEEM).

## Sample System and Motivation

The FeMn/Co bilayer system on Cu(001) represents an ideal model system for studying FM-AFM exchange coupling due to the well-defined crystallographic relationships that can be established through epitaxial growth. The face-centered cubic (fcc) FeMn antiferromagnet, when grown on Co/Cu(001), exhibits multiple crystallographic domain variants due to the symmetry breaking imposed by the underlying substrate and ferromagnetic layer. Critically, the AFM ordering in FeMn couples to the ferromagnetic Co layer through interfacial exchange interactions, and this coupling manifests as distinct magnetic domains within the Co layer that reflect different crystallographic easy-axis orientations. This provides a unique opportunity to study, within a single sample, how the local crystallographic environment influences the magnetic anisotropy and spectroscopic response of the ferromagnetic layer.

## Experimental Approach

To probe this system, we utilized synchrotron-based X-ray absorption spectroscopy combined with PEEM, which allows for simultaneous chemical and magnetic domain imaging with sub-micron spatial resolution. XMCD, sensitive to the projection of magnetic moments along the X-ray propagation direction, was employed to map the ferromagnetic domain structure of the Co layer, exploiting the strong circular dichroism at the Co L-edges arising from spin-orbit coupling in the presence of magnetization. Simultaneously, XMLD measurements were performed at the Fe L-edges to probe the antiferromagnetic order and its coupling to the underlying crystallographic structure, as XMLD is sensitive to the magnetic axis (rather than direction) and is therefore capable of detecting antiferromagnetic order even in the absence of net magnetization.

## Key Findings

### Domain-Dependent XMLD Contrast

A central finding of this work is the observation of a pronounced difference in XMLD contrast between magnetic domains associated with different crystallographic easy-axis orientations in the Co layer. This result was initially unexpected, as XMLD is traditionally associated with antiferromagnetic materials or systems with pronounced quadrupolar charge distributions. However, our careful analysis reveals that this contrast originates from the intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy of the ferromagnetic Co layer itself. The different crystallographic domains, induced by the coupling to the underlying FeMn antiferromagnet, exhibit distinct electronic and magnetic environments that manifest as measurable differences in the linear dichroism signal. This finding underscores the sensitivity of XMLD not only to antiferromagnetic ordering but also to the local crystallographic and magnetic anisotropy landscape within ferromagnetic thin films.

### Detection of Induced Fe Moments

Perhaps the most significant outcome of this study is the demonstration that XMLD can be used to detect extremely subtle induced ferromagnetic moments at the Fe/Co interface. Due to the direct exchange coupling between the FeMn antiferromagnet and the Co ferromagnet, a small ferromagnetic moment is induced in the interfacial Fe atoms, even though bulk FeMn remains antiferromagnetically ordered. This induced moment, while too weak to be reliably detected through conventional XMCD measurements at this interface, produces a measurable and consistent XMLD signal. This represents a significant methodological advance, as it establishes that XMLD imaging can achieve magnetic contrast sensitivity sufficient to detect weak, induced ferromagnetic order in a purely metallic system—a capability not previously well-established for such systems, where the technique has historically been more readily applied to oxide antiferromagnets with stronger intrinsic anisotropic charge distributions.

## Implications and Significance

These results have important implications for the broader field of magnetic thin film characterization and exchange-coupled systems. First, they demonstrate that XMLD-PEEM is a powerful complementary tool to XMCD for studying not only antiferromagnetic domain structures but also subtle magneto-crystalline anisotropy effects within ferromagnetic layers themselves. Second, the successful detection of induced interfacial ferromagnetic moments via XMLD opens new avenues for studying interfacial magnetism in metallic exchange-coupled systems, where such moments play a crucial role in mediating exchange bias and other interfacial phenomena, yet are often difficult to detect using conventional techniques due to their small magnitude and localization at buried interfaces.

## Conclusion

This study demonstrates the power of combined XMCD/XMLD-PEEM microscopy for investigating single-crystalline FeMn/Co bilayers on Cu(001), revealing both a substantial domain-dependent XMLD contrast attributable to Co magneto-crystalline anisotropy and, more significantly, the successful detection of weak induced ferromagnetic Fe moments at the FM-AFM interface. These findings establish XMLD as a sensitive probe not only for classical antiferromagnetic order but also for subtle magnetic and electronic anisotropies in metallic ferromagnetic systems, extending the applicability of this technique to a broader range of exchange-coupled thin film architectures relevant to spintronic device development.

# Investigating Magnetic Properties of FeMn Alloys Using XMCD and XMLD Spectroscopy

## Introduction

Iron-manganese (FeMn) alloys represent a class of materials with significant importance in spintronics and magnetic multilayer systems, primarily due to their antiferromagnetic ordering. These alloys are widely employed as pinning layers in exchange bias systems, where they interface with ferromagnetic layers to stabilize magnetic orientations in devices such as spin valves and magnetic tunnel junctions. Understanding the microscopic magnetic behavior of FeMn requires sophisticated element-specific characterization techniques, among which X-ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism (XMCD) and X-ray Magnetic Linear Dichroism (XMLD) have emerged as indispensable tools.

## X-ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism (XMCD)

XMCD exploits the differential absorption of left- and right-circularly polarized X-rays by magnetized materials. This technique is particularly sensitive to ferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic ordering, as it directly probes the net magnetic moment associated with an element. In the context of FeMn alloys, XMCD measurements are typically performed to assess residual ferromagnetic components or induced magnetization at interfaces, especially in exchange-biased FeMn/ferromagnet heterostructures. Since bulk FeMn is intrinsically antiferromagnetic, a vanishing or minimal XMCD signal in the alloy's interior confirms the absence of net magnetization, while any measurable signal often indicates uncompensated spins at grain boundaries or interfaces—a phenomenon closely linked to the exchange bias effect.

## X-ray Magnetic Linear Dichroism (XMLD)

Unlike XMCD, XMLD is sensitive to the antiferromagnetic order parameter itself, as it arises from the anisotropy of the absorption cross-section with respect to linearly polarized light and the local spin axis orientation. This makes XMLD the technique of choice for directly imaging antiferromagnetic domains in FeMn layers. By analyzing the dichroic signal as a function of the sample's magnetic history and applied field-cooling procedures, researchers can map the antiferromagnetic domain structure and correlate it with the ferromagnetic layer's magnetization direction in coupled systems.

## Combined XMCD-XMLD Studies of FeMn Systems

The complementary nature of XMCD and XMLD makes their combined application particularly powerful for FeMn-based exchange bias systems. While XMCD reveals information about induced or parasitic ferromagnetic moments, XMLD provides direct insight into the antiferromagnetic domain configuration that governs the pinning mechanism. Photoemission electron microscopy (PEEM) combined with XMLD contrast has enabled real-space imaging of antiferromagnetic domains in FeMn films, revealing domain sizes, orientations, and their correlation with the overlying ferromagnetic layer's domain structure.

Such studies have demonstrated that the antiferromagnetic domain structure in FeMn is not static but can be manipulated through thermal treatment, field cooling, and even by the ferromagnetic layer itself via interfacial coupling. This interplay is crucial for understanding training effects, thermal stability, and the microscopic origins of exchange bias in these systems.

## Conclusion

The combined use of XMCD and XMLD spectroscopy has substantially advanced the understanding of FeMn alloys' magnetic behavior, particularly at interfaces relevant to spintronic applications. These element-specific and order-parameter-sensitive techniques continue to provide critical insights into the fundamental mechanisms governing exchange bias, antiferromagnetic domain dynamics, and interfacial magnetism—knowledge essential for the continued development of next-generation magnetic storage and sensing technologies.

We report the detection of induced ferromagnetic Fe moments at the interface of an FeMn/Co exchange-biased bilayer system using X-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD) combined with photoemission electron microscopy (PEEM).
